cases.title: From Bagehot's merchant borrowing advantage to implicit bank funding guarantees

provenance.source_scope: Bagehot 1873 primary merchant arithmetic; IMF 2014 and 2013 studies motivate the conceptual public guarantee/discipline hypothesis. All loan rates, probabilities, guarantees, productivity, bank losses and policy choices in this case are synthetic and have no empirical calibration.
provenance.event_date_note: 2014-04-09 is an IMF paper-publication marker, not the date of a funding crisis.

observations: SYNTHETIC LAW: A representative bank borrows at a one-period risk-free gross return 1+r_f and has independently stipulated risk-neutral bank failure probability p_B and creditor recovery fraction R_B.
The Treasury may make a fraction g of promised bank-debt shortfall whole in bank default. Exactly at issue, competitive risk-neutral bank creditors require (1+r_B) [1-p_B (1-R_B)(1-g)] = 1+r_f.
This guarantee is on bank FUNDING claims. It differs from a central-bank collateralized liquidity loan, a merchant-loan guarantee, and a public bank common-equity recapitalization.

An underwriting intermediary passes fraction alpha of the reduction in its bank-funding rate into merchant credit. A zero-pass-through arm retains the cheaper funding inside the bank rather than lowering the merchant quote.
Bagehot's original 1873 10% versus 30% ROE example is a comparison at fixed operating profit and fixed scale. Here default risk and debt choice vary; all added behavioral laws are invented.
questions: Derive r_B = (1+r_f)/(1-p_B(1-R_B)(1-g))-1 and prove under positive denominator and risk-free gross rate that it is nonincreasing in g at fixed bank failure probability.
State the exact zero-pass-through and zero-bank-default-risk negative controls. Identify who benefits economically when the lending bank retains the lower funding cost.

Give an empirical identification strategy for rescue support expectations, funding spreads and merchant pass-through, separating them from bank size, collateral, default risk, fixed effects and the policy regime.

observations: NEW SYNTHETIC DECISION: the merchant owns GBP 10,000 equity and chooses debt on a GBP 5,000 ladder from zero through GBP 40,000, and chooses either prudent or aggressive project.

Project failure probability rises linearly in its chosen debt/equity ratio. A prudent project offers lower success-state operating returns and lower default risk. An aggressive project has higher success-state revenue with higher failure risk.

In success, assets must cover the promised debt amount. In failure, the lender recovers a stated fraction of promised debt, leaving the merchant with zero terminal equity. A full-repayment assumption in success is checked before scoring.

Merchant interest prices are chosen to cover loan losses under the assumed merchant-failure probability, with stated bank origination margin. The representative merchant chooses a strategy maximizing expected terminal shareholder value.

The bank-failure probability in the feedback arm is an explicitly chosen function of merchant project failure and leverage; each full portfolio is re-quoted before selecting the best plan. This is an enumerated conditional choice, not a price-taking general equilibrium.
questions: Compute the complete debt/project argmax for each specified coverage g. Give exact input units, both default probabilities, bank funding rate, merchant loan rate, chosen debt and expected shareholder profit.

Compare policy outcomes with alpha=0 and bank default probability equal to zero. Check for the presence and size of loan balance expansion and risk appetite changes rather than assuming every project becomes riskier.
Describe what additional model would be required to study millions of atomistic merchants where each takes the common bank funding price as given.

observations: NEW SYNTHETIC FISCAL EXPOSURE: if a bank defaults in the one-period model, Treasury pays g times the stipulated unsecured bank-funding creditor shortfall. Expected payout is bank PD times conditional guarantee payout on the bank-funding face value.

The bank funds the chosen merchant loan using a stipulated share of debt liabilities and the remainder common equity. That capital funding share does not automatically replenish a later loan impairment.

Every guarantee choice changes the terms offered at new bank-debt origination under the model. Conditional rescue payments are distinct from a public capital subscription, a central-bank credit loss, and a discretionary private-sector bail-in.

A second invented calibration changes the prudent project success-state return to test whether bank guarantees can also make a relatively safer project more attractive. With no known market data, the sign of the project-mix effect remains a model output.
questions: Calculate the expected Treasury exposure on guaranteed bank funding claims at the chosen portfolio and show why zero coverage implies zero guarantee payout.

Hold aggregate bank funding debt fixed while varying agent count; contrast fixed per-agent lending where total guarantees scale with the number of represented borrowers, conditional on fixed default parameters.
Explain how underwriting, bank capital rules, resolution with bail-in, merchant competition and guaranteed creditor behavior might break the proposed repeated recapitalization mechanism.
Separate a proved algebraic rate effect from the empirical question of whether past bank rescues changed observed funding costs and borrower behavior.

scoring_rules.decision_rule: maximize terminal expected merchant-equity profit; smaller debt and prudent project break ties

rubric_anchors: At fixed PD and LGD and positive denominator, a greater guarantee reduces the actuarially fair promised bank-debt interest rate.
Bank pass-through is an additional parameter; beta/alpha zero removes merchant rate movement across guarantee scenarios at identical risk composition.
Leveraged project selection depends on expected risk-adjusted terminal equity payout, which may differ from accounting ROE and Bagehot's fixed-profit illustration.
Fiscal guarantee exposure is state-contingent bank-debt coverage, distinct from bank common-equity injections or central-bank own capital restoration.
Credit supply and risk change through a synthetic decision rule; no inference of real-world subsidy size or welfare is authorized.
Conditional negative controls test zero default, zero pass-through, fixed/feedback bank PD, and project-mix ambiguity.
Two competing explanations of risk-taking effects include impaired market discipline and increased charter value.
